context:
On the Ask page, where the learner can also send written feedback to the editors.
Issues played: 1 Phở and friends; 2 Big numbers and prices; 3 One to ten, properly; 4 People and family; 5 At the market; 6 At the table; 7 Getting around; 8 A numbers clinic; 9 Your turn to haggle; 10 Hello in six tones; 11 So hot, so cold; 12 I want to ...; 13 Where is the market?.
Words the learner has met: gà (chicken), bò (beef; cow), cá (fish), trăm (hundred), nghìn (thousand), triệu (million), mươi (-ty, the tens (as in 20)), lăm (five, after the tens (as in 15 and 25)), linh (zero (for an empty tens place, as in 105)), rưỡi (and a half (after a unit)), tiền (money), bao nhiêu (how much, how many), đắt (expensive), rẻ (cheap), hơn (-er; more (after the describing word: cheap + more = cheaper)), nữa (more, another), bốn (four), tám (eight), chín (nine (also: ripe, cooked)), ba (three), một (one), hai (two), năm (five (also: year)), sáu (six), bảy (seven), mười (ten), tên (name), tôi (I, me (neutral; safe with strangers)), anh (older brother; you (to a man a bit older)), chị (older sister; you (to a woman a bit older)), em (younger brother or sister; you (to someone younger)), cô (aunt; you (to a woman a bit younger than your parents)), chú (uncle; you (to a man a bit younger than your parents)), ông (grandfather; you (to an old man)), bạn (friend; you (to someone your own age)), bà (grandmother; you (to an old woman)), mua (to buy), quả (fruit; also the counting word for fruit), cam (orange (the fruit)), chuối (banana), cân (a kilo; also: scale, to weigh), thịt (meat), bớt (to take some off (a price); to reduce), hết (in total (of a bill); also: used up, sold out), mời (to invite; please (go ahead, have some)), cháu (grandchild, niece or nephew; I (to your parents' or grandparents' generation)), bát (bowl (a rice bowl)), đũa (chopsticks), canh (soup (a clear broth eaten with rice)), no (full (after eating)), vâng (yes (polite, to someone older)), uống (to drink), xe ôm (motorbike taxi), đâu (where), trái (left (the side)), gần (near, close by), rẽ (to turn (at a corner)), phải (right (the side)), nhăm (five after the tens, a casual spoken form of lăm (as in 25)), mốt (one at the end of 21, 31 ... 91 (11 stays mười một)), tư (four at the end of 24, 34 ... 94 (14 stays mười bốn)), chục (a set of ten things, as sellers count (ten eggs)), hàng (wares, goods; a shop or stall that sells them), được (OK, all right; can be done), lấy (to take; I'll have (at a stall or at the table)), trứng (egg), chào (hello; goodbye), biết (to know (a fact, or how to do something)), khỏe (well, healthy; strong), xin lỗi (sorry; excuse me), gặp (to meet (someone)), nóng (hot), rét (cold (of the weather, and how you feel in it)), đẹp (beautiful, pretty; good-looking), đói (hungry), nấu (to cook), xem (to watch; to look at), ngủ (to sleep), muốn (to want (to)), quán (a small eatery, café or bar), nhà (house; home), chợ (a market), hồ (a lake).
Words they already knew: phở, cơm, bún, bánh mì, rau, nước, trà, cà phê, ngon, đồng.
Words still weak: nghìn, bao nhiêu, hơn, tên, ông, cam, chuối, cháu, đũa, canh, xe ôm, đâu, lấy, nấu, xem, muốn, chợ, hồ.

turns.text: Quán means a small eatery, café or bar in Vietnamese.
Bạn có muốn đi quán phở không? (slow) Bạn có muốn đi quán phở không? means "Do you want to go to a pho restaurant?"
"Bạn" means "friend," or "you" when speaking to someone roughly your own age.
And if you are someone older I'd say and if you're someone younger I'd say M.
That's right. You'd use "chị" for a woman a bit older, and "em" for someone younger.
You would likely use "cô". Cô means "aunt" and is also used to address a woman a bit younger than your parents.
Correct! You'd use "cô". So, cô có muốn đi quán phở không? (slow) Cô có muốn đi quán phở không? means "Do you want to go to the pho restaurant?"
